To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
mice from an artificial selective breeding experiment for high voluntary running behavior have a concomitantly larger femoral nutrient canal area than non‐selected mice.

mice with an evolutionarily recent history of increased locomotion and maximal aerobic metabolic capacity have larger femoral nutrient canal areas than control mice, and this is the result of increased canal size, not an increase in canal numbers.

(a) mice from lines selected for high voluntary wheel running had larger nutrient canals in their femora than control mice, (b) the increase in nutrient canal size was not due to an increase in the total number of canals, but was instead due to a larger average cross‐sectional size of each canal, and (c) the size of a mouse femur’s nutrient canals was correlated with the size of its nutrient canal opening.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between bone structure and locomotor performance.
the evolution of bone nutrient canals and their relationship with locomotor activity.
the evolution and function of the nutrient canal of the long bones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mice with an evolved history of high aerobic physical activity have larger nutrient canals than mice with an evolved background of low aerobic physical activity.
the size of the femoral nutrient canal in mice is a skeletal indicator of maximal aerobic metabolic rate and physical activity, but that the primary determinant of canal size is not well‐understood.
the nutrient canals are more numerous and larger in HR mice than C mice, which suggests a greater blood flow in the former.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mice with high levels of voluntary wheel‐running activity have larger nutrient canals in their femora.
mice with an increased capacity for aerobic metabolism have a larger nutrient canal size, which is indicative of an increased capacity for blood supply.
the size of the femoral nutrient canal is a skeletal proxy of maximal aerobic capacity in mice, which is consistent with the idea that bone is an oxygen‐consuming tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nutrient canal is an important and underappreciated skeletal proxy of bone blood flow.
the nutrient canal is a highly variable structure that can provide a useful skeletal indicator of blood flow into long bone.

the nutrient canal system is more complicated than previously thought, and that the number and shape of these nutrient canals are likely to be influenced by a variety of factors, including the size and shape of the bone, the location of the canal within the bone, and the genetic background of the animal.
